articles.title: The Way Science Progresses
articles.summary: This article discusses the iterative and self-correcting nature of scientific progress, emphasizing that initial findings often require independent verification and additional data to be confirmed or refuted. It illustrates this process with historical and contemporary examples, including debates surrounding Gliese 581's exoplanets, cold fusion, Edwin Hubble's red shift data, stellar parallax measurements, the nature of spiral nebulae, and NASA's announcement of arsenic-based life. The document also includes the San Jose Astronomical Association's activity calendar for January and February 2011.

articles.title: The Shallow Sky
articles.summary: This article from early 2011 provides an update on evening sky observations, noting Jupiter's prominence and the return of its South Equatorial Band, along with the visibility of Uranus and Neptune. It also includes Mars Rover news, detailing ongoing efforts to re-establish contact with Spirit and Opportunity's continued exploration towards Santa Maria crater.

articles.title: Hubble 2010
articles.summary: The article "Hubble 2010" showcases a selection of top astronomical images released by NASA and the Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI) in 2010, as highlighted by Caroline Hirsch for the New Yorker. It details several breathtaking captures from the Hubble Space Telescope, including the Carina Nebula's star-forming regions, a multi-observatory composite of the Antennae galaxies, and the spiral galaxy NGC 3982.

articles.title: NASA Space Place
articles.summary: Using NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope, astronomers have discovered large, three-dimensional carbon molecules known as fullerenes—including "buckyballs" (C60) and C70—in a planetary nebula. These are the largest known molecules in space, suggesting that complex carbonaceous chemistry can occur spontaneously and potentially holding implications for the formation of life in the universe.

articles.title: New Logo
articles.summary: The article announces a new logo for the Ephemeris, designed by Peter Natscher and approved by the board in November. It also details an upcoming "Astronomy 10A: An Introduction to the Planets & Life Out There" course at Foothill College, taught by Andrew Fraknoi. This introductory course for non-science majors covers topics such as exoplanets, dwarf planets, and the latest planetary discoveries, and is set to begin in the Winter Quarter on January 3rd.

articles.title: The Last Month In Astronomy
articles.summary: This article summarizes recent astronomical findings from late 2010. It details Voyager 1's approach to interstellar space, new WISE observations revealing unusual composition in the supernova remnant IC 443, and an updated estimate for the universe's total star count, significantly increased by abundant red dwarfs in elliptical galaxies. Additionally, it covers the study of exoplanet GJ1214b, found to have a low density and an atmosphere dominated by water vapor.

articles.title: It Must Be Astronomical...
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) newsletter provides updates on their loaner telescope program and an upcoming dues change effective January 1, 2011, which differentiates between electronic and print newsletter subscribers. It also promotes the "Astronomy Cast" podcast and details statistics for past and upcoming "School Star Parties." The article concludes with a list of SJAA officers, board members, and contact information for the association and its monthly publication, "SJAA Ephemeris."
